newsitem.title: FRANCE: Santer denies Commission misleading over BSE.
newsitem.headline: Santer denies Commission misleading over BSE.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer denied on Wednesday that the EU executive had ever put the interests of the beef market before public health or tried to play down the dangers of BSE.

Responding to a European Parliament committee of inquiry into the crisis caused by Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), he said the Commission was planning to take steps to separate the responsibilities for food safety and agricultural policy to make sure problems could be avoided in future.

"My experience over the past two years at the head of the Commission makes me refuse the idea according to which we would have given priority to the market to the detriment of public health or carried out a deliberate policy of disinformation," he said in a prepared speech to the committee.
"That is not the case I can assure you. In all our discussions in the Commission our aim was to protect transparency and follow the scientific line and to avoid any risk for human health."
He said he doubted that the previous EU executive had been guilty of such acts either.
"As regards the management of the BSE crisis in the past I have great difficulty in believing that it behaved any differently," he said.

But he said that following an internal review prompted by the row over the handling of the mad cow crisis the responsibility for food health could be brought under one roof rather than several as at present.
Under the plan responsibility could be given to European Commissioner for Consumer Policy Emma Bonino, he said

He admitted that due to the uncertainty at the time -- when BSE was considered to be an animal disease and scientists themselves had hesitated over what to do -- it had been difficult to know how to react to the crisis.
"This matter should be a lesson in modesty and humility," he said.

The parliamentary committee's draft report accuses the Commission of trying to play down the dangers of BSE which caused consumer panic and a crisis in the beef industry when Britain announced last year that it could be transmitted to humans in the form of Creutzfeld Jakob Disease.
He said that in order to ensure that those applying the rules and those making sure they were applied were not one and the same, an independent European agency should be set up.
He stressed EU governments had been reluctant to set up such an agency in the past.
